posts.title: Total eclipse of the art: The beautiful undertones of moonlit paintings
posts.description: As so often, it was the ancient Greeks who first settled the matter. In the 5th century BC, the philosopher Anaxagoras conclusively determined that moonlight is reflected sunlight. This realisation helped to reinforce the character of the moon as a symbol. Presiding over the night and waxing and waning through the course of a month, it was thought of as the sister of the sun, mutable and feminine, whereas the sun was conceived of as an unchanging masculine force of Nature. Moonlight, which seems blue or silver to human eyes, had an important practical value in the centuries before large-scale artificial light, as it allowed work to continue after sunset, but it was also perceived to have powerful mystical or supernatural qualities. The word ‘lunatic’ is derived from the Latin word for the moon, luna, and the full moon was believed to give birth to ghosts and spirits, as well as werewolves. posts.title: Most of the grandest gardens at the Belle Époque villas of the Riviera are either gone or locked away — Villa Ephrussi is a wonderful exception
posts.description: Baroness Charlotte Beatrix de Rothschild (Béatrice to friends and family) spent much of her childhood at the Château de Ferrières, built for her grandfather James de Rothschild by none other than Joseph Paxton — the landscape gardener-turned-architect of Chatsworth’s glasshouses in Derbyshire and Crystal Palace in London. Inside, the lavishly decorated rooms contained an exceptional collection of fine art, tapestries, and furnishings from le grand siècle , as, outside, beyond the formal terracing, Paxton laid out a pastoral idyll of carefully framed views that guided the eye to a picturesque lake and manicured parkland. It may all have been designed to impress the Second Empire’s highest society, but it was young Béatrice perhaps, who was most deeply affected by those glorious surroundings. posts.title: You’ve Got Mail, and we’ve got the house: Meg Ryan's on-screen apartment is for sale
posts.description: The internet was at its most romantic — stick with me here — in the 1990s. When it still felt new and exciting and full of endless possibilities, and less like it and its tech bro gatekeepers might bring about the end of civilisation. It is a thought best exemplified by You’ve Got Mail (1998), a film in which two characters fall in love with each other through words, exchanged via then novel electronic message. Online dating was still in its most primitive form, and Tinder wasn’t even a twinkle in its founder’s eye. Oh, the good old days. The film, which is most definitely in my top ten of all time, isn’t a Christmas film proper, but moves from autumn into the festive season, capturing New York at its most enchanting. And now, as if by magic, you can purchase the Upper West Side townhouse that had a starring role in it — and some 1990s nostalgia to boot — just in time for December 25.
